Peoria 1956 Address Finder

Created by Tony Brocksmith & Claude for the Memories of Peoria Facebook Group. October 2026

Look up the old and new house numbers from the city's 1956 street-renumbering change sheets. Search by name, by the old address, or by the new address. Every result shows its change-sheet page number and where to find it in the PDF.

Download the complete 1956 change sheets (PDF, 22 MB, 712 pages)

Type a last name, or a first and last name. Partial names work.

Streets renamed in 1956

Many streets got new names along with new numbers. These come from the change sheets' headings and "(formerly …)" notes. Click an old name to list its addresses.

Reading the listings

About the spellings. The listings were read from typed carbon sheets, so some names and street names may be slightly off. If a search finds nothing, try fewer letters, only the last name, or only the house number and street.

A different street name. Some buildings got a new number on a different street, usually because they sit on a corner or their door faces the cross street. For example, 703 Spencer St. became 203 N. Sheridan Rd. A few streets were also renamed outright, such as E. Cox Ave. to E. Crestwood Dr. A new street name is a real change, not a typo.

The N., S., E. or W. before the street. All streets are numbered north or south from Aiken Avenue, or east or west from Knoxville Avenue. The city's instructions say this letter is part of the street name and should be used. That is why 544 Peoria Ave. became 2000 N. Peoria Ave. Some addresses already fit the new system and kept their number, gaining only the letter, as when 401 Fifth Ave. became 401 W. Fifth Ave.

Who is named. The sheets list the person living at each address. For vacant buildings, apartments and new construction, they list the owner instead, as in "Vacant (Owner: …)" or "Const. (Owner: …)". The person named may not be the person who lived there.

"(County)" instead of a name. These are properties outside the city limits that were renumbered along with the city. The sheets don't name the residents.

Numbers ending in X. The sheets don't define it, but an X marks a second building on the same lot, usually a rear house or a half-numbered address. It takes the main house's number with an X added. For example, on one sheet 1438 became 2618, and 1438 Rear became 2618X. So 2209X is most likely a building behind or beside 2209. The main house with the same number is usually listed right next to it.

What the page code means. The change sheets are grouped by quarter-section areas of the city's key map. In 33-D-8, "33-D" is the map area and "8" is the sheet number within it. Pages marked "April-56-Misc." are a separate group for changes outside the main renumbering area. The key map is included near the front of the collection.

Streets not in this finder. About three-quarters of Peoria's streets were renumbered in 1956. The main exceptions were the older streets along the Illinois River, which run at a 45-degree angle to the rest of the city and kept their old numbers. Some other streets already fit the new grid and were not renumbered. The area north of McClure Avenue was renumbered a year earlier, in 1955, so most of those addresses are not here. The project changed about 21,000 addresses in all, and this collection holds about 15,500, so some 1956 changes may be missing. If you can't find a family or building, the reason may be one of these, not the spelling.

Source. Download the complete change sheets (PDF). City of Peoria, Office of the City Engineer, street number change sheets effective May 11, 1956, with Correction Sheets #21–#29 (May 10–11, 1956) and Errata Sheets 8 and 9 applied. Under city ordinances and by resolution of the City Council, the City Engineer assigned these numbers to fit the uniform grid system. Background on the streets left unchanged and the total number of changes comes from "Street Names, Numbers Get New Look in Peoria," a 1956 article in Illinois Municipal Review (Illinois Periodicals Online, Northern Illinois University). Banner image: "Spalding Institute, Peoria, Ill.," 1910 postcard, courtesy of the McLean County Museum of History (McLean County Historical Society).
